newsitem.title: UK: ERM membership risky for UK - Goldman's Davies.
newsitem.headline: ERM membership risky for UK - Goldman's Davies.

text.p: It would be dangerous for Britain to rejoin the EU's exchange rate mechanism at the moment, Gavyn Davies, managing director and chief international economist at Goldman Sachs International told a conference on Wednesday.
"To join would be a very risky thing," Davies said.
Davies is widely tipped to be appointed to a deputy governorship at the Bank of England.
He said that joining the ERM at a central rate of 2.50 to 2.60 mark with 15 percent bands would capture all the movement in sterling over the past six years.

But achieving such a level would be hard: "First of all, getting a 2.50 exchange rate agreed with the rest of Europe and then keeping it within implied narrow bands (around 2.50) would be tricky," he said.
Britain's new Labour government, which ousted the Conservatives on May 1, has adopted a more enthusiastic attitude towards Europe, Davies said. Davies has long been an adviser to the Labour Party.

He noted the new government's renewed commitment to join the EU's Social Chapter on workers rights and secondly, the decision to give the Bank of England operational independence, removed one of the major obstacles to EMU membership.

"The government could signal an intention to participate in EMU by rejoining the ERM, but such a move is unlikely before 1998, although the government could move more quickly," he said in his speech to Goldman Sachs' annual foreign exchange conference.
"We are going to get a change in policy stance (on EMU) with no timetable and no near-term re-entry to the ERM," he said.

But he argued that holding a referendum on EMU entry, as promised by Labour, could pose a stumbling block to entry. He said opinion polls showed around 60 percent of Britons were against it whilst only just over 20 percent were in favour, with the rest undecided.
